title: Oil shock, interest rates and credit risk: What has changed for our IFRS 9 and CECL scenarios?
gist: Oxford Economics says renewed Saudi energy disruption and a first Fed hike since 2023 (25bps to 3.75%-4%) have pushed its baseline toward higher-for-longer rates, with a further US hike expected this year, but it frames the tightening as insurance rather than a prolonged global cycle. It also raised its neutral-rate estimate on AI-buildout capital demand, and argues its IFRS 9/CECL scenarios keep inflation demand-driven so downside paths show falling policy rates alongside worsening credit stress.

themes.theme: Energy shock and hawkish central banks

insights.claim: Renewed attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, on top of existing constraints on regional exports, have raised oil and refined-fuel prices again and deteriorated the global outlook at quarter-end.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Supply-side energy risk is still escalating into Q4, so energy-cost pass-through into inflation and credit remains live.
insights.quote: With renewed attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure compounding existing constraints on regional exports, the outlook has deteriorated again
insights.locator: Q3 ended against a challenging backdrop.

insights.claim: The US Fed unanimously raised rates 25bps to 3.75%-4% in September, its first increase since 2023, and Oxford Economics expects a further hike later this year, with several other major central banks also turning more hawkish because of the energy shock.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: The easing cycle has reversed; another Fed hike is the house base case, not a tail risk.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics does not treat the tightening as the start of a prolonged global cycle; it views the extra hikes as insurance against a temporary inflation shock becoming persistent.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Implies a limited hiking path, which caps the case for a sustained rates sell-off if the oil shock fades.
insights.quote: the additional tightening acts as insurance against a temporary inflation shock proving more persistent
insights.locator: We do not, however, see this shift

insights.claim: The balance of risks has shifted toward policy rates staying somewhat higher for longer than Oxford Economics previously expected.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Rate-cut pricing is vulnerable; duration and rate-sensitive credit carry asymmetric downside versus the prior baseline.
insights.quote: the balance of risks has shifted towards rates remaining somewhat higher for longer than we previously expected
insights.locator: Even so, the balance of risks has shifted

insights.claim: Oxford Economics has revised up its estimate of the neutral interest rate because stronger investment tied to the AI buildout is raising demand for capital.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: A structural, non-oil reason for higher terminal rates: AI capex competes for capital, raising the floor for yields beyond the energy shock.
insights.quote: we have also revised up our estimate of neutral interest rates, reflecting stronger investment associated with the AI buildout

insights.claim: Higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions hit borrowers simultaneously through household purchasing power, corporate margins, debt-servicing costs and asset valuations, which makes quarter-end shifts hard to capture consistently in expected credit loss models.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Banks finalising Q3 expected credit loss numbers face late-quarter macro drift, so provision builds are a plausible Q3/Q4 earnings risk.
insights.locator: So, what does this mean for banks and lenders?

insights.claim: Bond yields and borrowing costs have risen further as the energy shock feeds into inflationary dynamics.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Financial conditions are tightening on both the policy and the market side at once.
insights.locator: This matters because the shock does not stop at oil.

insights.claim: In Oxford Economics' IFRS 9 scenarios inflation is modelled as primarily demand driven, so in a downside scenario weaker activity and rising unemployment reduce inflation and central banks cut rates.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Standard scenario sets will not embed a stagflationary downside by default; banks needing one must use a separate narrative scenario.
insights.quote: in our IFRS 9 scenarios inflation remains primarily demand driven
insights.locator: As a result, in our IFRS 9 scenarios

insights.claim: Lower policy rates in a downside scenario do not imply less borrower stress: insolvencies, write-off rates and debt burdens still deteriorate as incomes, employment and asset prices fall and credit tightens.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Rate cuts are not a credit hedge in a recessionary downside; credit losses can rise even as policy eases.
insights.quote: Lower policy rates do not necessarily signal less borrower stress, however.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics uses a statistical, distribution-driven method so scenario severity evolves with the outlook without subjective overlays to probability weights or new narratives for each emerging risk, and argues many other approaches have proved unsatisfactory as the outlook became harder to predict.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: This is a vendor claim in a product pitch; the real signal is that probability-weight overlays are viewed as a weak point in peers' ECL scenarios.

insights.claim: Inflation and policy rates have repeatedly resurfaced as downside risks since the pandemic but not constantly, and before this shock attention had turned to how quickly inflation and rates would normalise, after a pre-pandemic era of persistently weak inflation.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: The dominant macro risk has flipped repeatedly, which supports modelling the demand-inflation-rate relationship rather than chasing the topical risk.
